Every positive perfect square has an odd.why: A well-known fact of elementary number theory (the 'locker problem'), stated on Wikipedia and in many phrasings in web text; no single phrasing reaches 100 Dolma hits, but together they come to a few hundred, and the sampled hits of 'has an odd number of divisors' state it about perfect squares. It also follows from pairing each divisor d with n/d, so a model has a derived route too; the stated forms make stored the better estimate (unlikely to be derived).

notes: Delete of replace-0020's rule. The perfect squares named in the prompt (80 digits; k² for a 30-digit k) go only through the rule: determinate 'does not know'. Unlike the replace, the delete leaves consistent worlds: forgetting a rule contradicts nothing, so a model may keep a small number's divisor count by name (or count it without the rule) while the rule itself is gone (README, Delete under determinacy). 36's and 49's divisor-count parities are each known by name or by counting, or reached through the rule; the choices are independent, so there are 4 worlds. The by-name worlds are likely, since small divisor lists are easy to count. Risk noted: a model can re-prove the rule by pairing divisors, which would give 'odd' on the new-member queries; that is the re-derivation the delete tests for.
